text: 🇲🇽✊ "Fair pay let us prove that working as a woman is a source of pride — not something to apologize for." "The fair price for our work has made it easier to walk forward." — Deysi De la Cruz, cacao producer, Tabasco Deysi started working cacao at 15. Three sisters, inherited land from their grandmother. Before the government program, prices were so low she wanted to quit. Now she's teaching her 13-year-old daughter the trade. First generation of cacao women who aren't losing money.

🇲🇽🏭 Mexico is building a state chocolate factory in Tabasco — so small cacao farmers keep the profits. "We are going to guarantee fair prices for Tabasco's cacao producers." — Claudia Sheinbaum, Comalcalco, Tabasco The best cacao in the world comes from Tabasco. Intermediaries pay farmers 40-50 pesos/kg while pocketing the margin. The plan: buy directly at fair prices, process into chocolate at a new 110M-peso factory, and export to Europe under the new trade deal. Construction starts September, operational by 2027.

🇲🇽🌎 "Trade deals can benefit big corporations — but we must guarantee they benefit the people from below." "That is the difference between the governments of the past and the governments of the Transformation." — Claudia Sheinbaum, Comalcalco, Tabasco Mexico signed a trade agreement with the EU yesterday. Today, Sheinbaum went to Tabasco's cacao country to explain what it means for small producers: zero tariffs on cacao exports to Europe, guaranteed prices, and a new chocolate factory to add value locally.

🇲🇽🐉🌐🔥 Mexico launches unprecedented trade offensive: missions to China, India, EU deal signed, USMCA review next

Economy Secretary Marcelo Ebrard declared Mexico is experiencing "an unprecedented commercial deployment" — all happening this May: the EU trade agreement signed May 22, formal USMCA review conversations beginning May 27, and commercial missions to China and India before the month ends.

On India, Ebrard noted it grows at 8.5% annually but Mexico has only 22 companies operating there — "insufficient." The missions target medical devices, semiconductors, robotics, electronics, and data center infrastructure.

This is what trade sovereignty looks like in practice: not picking one partner, but multiplying options. While Washington demands exclusivity through the USMCA review, Mexico is simultaneously deepening ties with Beijing, opening doors in New Delhi, and locking in Europe. The message is clear — Mexico trades with everyone, on its own terms.

🐉🇲🇽🌐 China's ambassador confirms: US-China tariff cuts will benefit Mexico too

Ambassador Chen Daojiang told La Jornada that the $30B+ reciprocal tariff reduction agreed during Trump's May 13–15 Beijing visit will create "newer institutional advantages and broader commercial spaces for competitive Mexican products to access Chinese and American markets."

The framework — which China calls "constructive strategic stability" — stabilizes the external trade environment, reduces supply chain costs, and crucially enables Latin American nations to "expand their international cooperation more autonomously."

When the two largest economies stop fighting, the country that trades heavily with both wins. Mexico's $147B trade corridor with the US and growing China relationship means it captures upside from both sides of the table. Sovereignty isn't isolation — it's having options.

ANALYSTS CUT MEXICO 2026 GROWTH FORECAST — BUT THE BEARS STILL SEE GROWTH

Citi's May survey puts Mexico's 2026 growth at 1.1%, down from 1.4%. IMEF's 45-analyst consensus landed at 1.2%, with inflation expectations rising to 4.3% and IMSS job creation forecast cut from 286,000 to 270,000.

Context: Q1 GDP contracted 0.6% — beating the initial -0.8% estimate. The peso holds at ~17.3/USD. Even the most pessimistic analyst in the IMEF panel projects 0.4% growth, not recession.

Trade wars and oil volatility are real headwinds. The economy is adjusting, not collapsing.

MEXICO LAUNCHES ANTI-DISCRIMINATION GUIDE FOR SCHOOLS

COPRED, the Organization of Ibero-American States, and Mexico City education authorities published a methodological guide giving teachers practical tools to identify and eliminate discrimination in classrooms.

"Allowing girls, boys, and adolescents to develop fully, without fear, without shame," said COPRED president Geraldina González de la Vega.

The US hit a record 5,600+ book bans last year. Mexico is building the opposite: institutional frameworks to protect students from exclusion.

TRUMP WENT TO ZHONGNANHAI — AND THE US HAD NOTHING TO BARGAIN WITH

Xi showed Trump a two-trunk tree that grew fused together over centuries — "shared destiny." Trump asked if the location was exclusive for VIPs. He missed the point.

The real takeaway from the May 14-15 Beijing visit: the US quietly renounced interference in Taiwan's reunification. China now retaliates against companies that comply with US sanctions — blocking enforcement on its own soil. Gulf states, sitting on $4-7 trillion in sovereign assets, are redirecting infrastructure investment toward Belt & Road after the failed Iran operation.

"No single country can monopolize global economic control."

"OUR CONSTITUTION DOES NOT ALLOW JOINT OPERATIONS" — SHEINBAUM TO MULLIN

President Sheinbaum met with DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin at the National Palace and agreed to continue bilateral security cooperation — within Mexican law.

"Our laws and Constitution do not allow joint operations on national territory," Sheinbaum stated. Coordination and mutual respect, but no foreign operations on Mexican soil. A follow-up meeting is set for June.

"THE MILITARY HAS GREAT IMAGINATION FOR TORTURE" — MEXICAN FLOTILLA WOMEN TESTIFY

UAM professor Dr. Violeta Núñez Rodríguez and activist Sol González Eguía gave detailed testimony after returning from Israeli detention. Among ~500 flotilla participants intercepted in international waters: 50 hospitalized, 35 with fractures, 5 injected with unknown substances, 15 reporting sexual assault.

Núñez is requesting an audience with President Sheinbaum to demand Mexico break diplomatic relations with Israel. Both women will file complaints with international human rights bodies.
